messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur Vance was in the sub-basement of the Grand Meridian Hotel, reviewing the winterization logs, when the pressure valve on the third-line boiler room fractured. The initial hiss of escaping solvent had been swallowed by the building’s ventilation, but the acrid, chemical-sweet stench hit him the moment he dropped his clipboard. His recollection offered no single sequence; only jagged, disconnected pieces—a flickering fluorescent tube, the slick grip of a steel ladder, the way his lungs burned in quick, shallow pulls. He tried to turn toward the exit, but his legs felt like dead weight, and the heavy iron door clicked shut behind him, sealing the vapor inside. In that dark, pressurized space, Arthur had come to believe he could not stop bad things from happening to him. He felt the full, suffocating panic of that night even now, though no clear image of the event would ever surface in his mind. Only the smell of burnt sugar and copper would return, unbidden and sharp, whenever his attention drifted toward the past. Over the following weeks, Arthur found himself on guard even inside his own house. The kitchen tiles and the study rugs offered no shelter; he could only relax in the back armchair by the fireplace, the one spot where the windows were painted shut and the air seemed still. At the hotel, his attention sharpened to the acoustics of service corridors. Every unexpected clank of a pipe, every dropped tray in the elevator shaft, sent his pulse rising. He sat rigid in his office while maintenance crews worked below, listening for the particular cadence of heavy boots. He filled the rooms with loud music or turned the television up to maximum volume, layering noise until there was no quiet left to navigate. Even in the din, he sifted through his own thoughts, checking for any sign that he was going crazy, any proof that the exposure had fractured his mind permanently. He stopped taking the service elevator entirely, walking two extra flights of stairs each morning just to put distance between himself and the boiler room. His body felt like an enemy, twitching at shadows, jumping at his own reflection, reacting as though the chemical air still filled the halls he walked through. He could no longer trust his own lungs or his nerves, only that they were lying to him about his safety. The distance he needed grew from miles into chasms. Over months, he delegated the night inspections to his assistant manager, then to someone else entirely, until his own office hours shrank to daylight. His ex-wife’s weekly calls went unanswered for seasons, then years, until the silence between them became as thick as the fumes he had breathed. He told himself he was protecting his staff from his growing irritability, but in truth, he was simply trying to outrun a threat that no longer had a location. He finally walked into the community mental health clinic last Tuesday, his pension paperwork clutched in one hand and a faded maintenance map of the city in the other, pointing to the condemned wing of the hotel. He did not want answers about his lungs. He wanted to know how to stop bracing for a collapse that would never come, and how to sit in a room where he might finally, safely, just listen to a record instead of filling the silence. He feared that if he let his guard down even once, the past would rush back in without warning, but he was hoping, however faintly, that someone might show him how to exist in a space where his body no longer sounded the alarm.
